extracted.intended_audience: beginners and intermediate users of the Coq proof assistant (students, programmers, formal-methods users)
extracted.subtask_description: Creating formal specifications, definitions and interactive proofs in the Coq proof assistant using the Gallina language and Coq tactics; includes module/section management, inductive types, and use of automation/classical axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer graphical interface (CoqIde) but shell is supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq can be used from a teletype-like shell but is preferably used through the graphical user interface CoqIde (other GUIs: Proof General, Pcoq).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tutorial examples assume the shell prompt 'Coq <'. When working interactively prefer CoqIde for usability; shell examples remain valid. Installation and further documentation are in the standard distribution and on the Coq website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always report the Coq version banner when filing bugs
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard invocation of coqtop prints a banner with the precise Coq version used; you should return this banner when you report an anomaly to the bug-tracking system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example banner: 'Welcome to Coq 8.2 (January 2009)'. Include it verbatim in bug reports so maintainers can reproduce issues with the same version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier naming rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers are strings of letters, digits and a few ASCII symbols (underscore, prime), must start with a letter, are case-sensitive; reserved keywords are forbidden as user identifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of case distinctions (A and a distinct). Avoid names that clash with Coq keywords.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of specifications/sorts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three basic kinds of specifications: logical propositions (Prop), mathematical collections (Set), and abstract types (Type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every Gallina expression e has a type τ(e); use 'Check' to inspect the type. Understand which sort (Prop/Set/Type) to use when declaring propositions, data types or abstract types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Check' to inspect expressions and types
rubrics_metrics.description: The Check command returns the type/specification of any valid expression in Gallina.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Check O.' prints ': nat'. Use Check on functions, propositions, and types to confirm expected sorts and arities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure developments with Section/End
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections delimit scope of parameters, hypotheses and definitions; closing a section generalises and discharges local hypotheses in resulting theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Section to group related declarations and End to emit generalized statements. Use Reset Declaration or 'Reset Initial' to revert global pollution. Sections are useful to avoid global axioms and to control dependencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce parameters and hypotheses with Variable and Hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare parameters (Variable name : type.) and logical assumptions (Hypothesis name : proposition.) to set up the local context for proofs/definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple names may be declared at once (Variables A B C : Prop.). Use Hypothesis for named assumptions you intend to discharge when the section is closed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition syntax and optional typing
rubrics_metrics.description: Define constants and functions with 'Definition name := expr.' or 'Definition name : type := expr.'; functions can be defined by explicit fun abstractions or parameter lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Definition double (m:nat) := plus m m.' or 'Definition two : nat := S one.' Use explicit type annotation when helpful for clarity or to guide inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid variable capture when renaming bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Bound (local) variables and free (global) variables may be mixed; renaming a bound variable to a name already free would capture that free occurrence and change meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When renaming formal arguments or bound variables, ensure no accidental capture of free names (e.g., don't rename parameter m to n if n is free in the body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit typing for quantified/bound variables
rubrics_metrics.description: In Gallina you must declare the type of quantified or abstracted variables (e.g., 'forall m:nat, ...' or 'fun x:A => e').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syntax requires types for all bound variables; e.g., 'forall m:nat, gt m 0'. This is important for well-formedness and typechecking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Goal/Lemma/Theorem to enter proof mode
rubrics_metrics.description: Start proofs with Goal, Lemma, or Theorem followed by the conjecture to enter Coq’s proof mode where tactics operate on the current goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Goal (A -> B -> C) -> (A -> B) -> A -> C.' shows current goal and local context; then use intro/intro to move premises to hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intro/Intros move premises to hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'intro' tactic moves the leftmost implication antecedent into a named hypothesis; 'intros' does as many introductions as possible (optionally naming them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'intro H.' or 'intros H1 H2.' Using intros with no args auto-generates non-clashing names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'apply' to use an hypothesis/lemma to reduce a goal
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'apply H' tactic attempts to match the conclusion of hypothesis H with the current goal, creating subgoals for H’s premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After apply you may get multiple subgoals corresponding to premises of the applied lemma/hypothesis. Use 'apply ... with <instantiation>' when some implicit arguments need explicit instantiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact and assumption to finish goals from available hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'exact H' finishes the goal if H matches the goal exactly; 'assumption' finishes the goal if it is present among local hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use exact when you have a proof term/hypothesis that precisely matches the goal; assumption is a convenience to search local hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacticals for composing tactics (sequencing and branching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'T1; T2' to run T1 then T2 on all subgoals; use 'T ; [T1|T2|...|Tn]' to run T then different tactics on each generated subgoal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'apply H; [ assumption | apply H0; assumption ]' applies H and then uses different tactics on the two subgoals produced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'auto' and extend its hint database via Hint Resolve
rubrics_metrics.description: 'auto' attempts to solve goals by using local hypotheses and lemmas registered as hints; it is efficient because it avoids expensive elimination steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Register lemmas with 'Hint Resolve lemma_name.' to be used by auto. Note: auto will not generally perform elimination (destruct/elim) steps, which can limit its power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'tauto' for propositional tautologies
rubrics_metrics.description: 'tauto' is a complete tactic for propositional tautologies (classical within Prop-level), and always returns an answer for such problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: tauto may fail on some classical tautologies in constructive logic; to use classical reasoning, import Classical or provide excluded middle axioms. You can Print a lemma to see the proof term produced by tauto.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical reasoning requires importing Classical or adding EM
rubrics_metrics.description: Coq is constructive by default; to use classical principles (excluded middle, double-negation elimination) you must Require Import Classical or assume EM/NNPP explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After 'Require Import Classical.' lemmas like NNPP are available. Alternatively, add local hypothesis 'Hypothesis EM : forall A:Prop, A \/ ~ A.' Use NNPP and tauto together to derive classical laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elimination (elim) and pattern-based tactics for connectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'elim H' to eliminate hypotheses built with /\/exists/inductive constructors; use 'split' to introduce conjunctions and 'left'/'right' to build disjunctions (or_introl/or_intror).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: elim breaks a hypothesis into cases; split creates conjunctive subgoals; left/right correspond to disjunction introductions. clear removes irrelevant hypotheses to declutter context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existential handling: ex, Exists, ex_intro and elimination yield witness
rubrics_metrics.description: Existential quantifier is ex A (fun x => P x); introduce an existential with 'Exists witness' (ex_intro) and eliminate it to obtain a witness a:D and hypothesis P a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example proof: from 'forall x, P x' and having a domain element d, conclude 'Exists d'—but be careful: Coq does not assume types are inhabited unless you provide a witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about inhabitedness of types when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike classical first-order logic, Coq does not assume domains (types) are non-empty; lemmas that require an element of a type must either be given a witness or be restricted to inhabited types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs like 'forall x, P x -> exists a, P a' require an explicit domain element (e.g., variable d : D). Use such witnesses or explicit hypotheses asserting inhabitedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'apply ... with <arg>' to instantiate otherwise-implicit arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: When apply cannot infer how to instantiate intermediate arguments, use 'apply Lemma with arg1 arg2' to supply those instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'apply R_transitive with y.' to tell apply how to choose the middle element y when proving transitivity-based goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use generalize and cut to manipulate goals and assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'generalize H' moves a hypothesis into the goal as an implication; 'cut (P)' introduces P as a new subgoal that you can prove separately and then use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use generalize to obtain a more general induction hypothesis; use cut to assert lemmas you plan to prove immediately after (keeps proof obligations explicit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive datatypes: define with Inductive; Coq generates elimination/induction principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive definitions (e.g., nat, bool) introduce constructors and automatically generate recursion and induction principles (nat_ind, nat_rec).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Fixpoint/match for recursive functions (with {struct ...} to indicate decreasing argument). Use Eval cbv beta to compute/β-reduce types or terms when printed forms are verbose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by induction: use elim/simple induction and the generated induction principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'elim n' or 'simple induction n' (which does the necessary intros) to perform structural induction, producing base and step subgoals corresponding to the induction principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with 'simpl' and 'auto' and register base lemmas with Hint Resolve. Example: prove properties of addition by induction on one argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discriminate to rule out equality between distinct constructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'discriminate' (or the discriminating predicate approach) to prove contradictions like O <> S n mechanically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatively, transform goals with 'change' to a computationally evaluating form and use simpl + trivial; discriminate automates this pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define inductive predicates to do logic programming; use generated induction principle for reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive predicates (e.g., le) are defined with clauses/constructors and Coq generates minimality/induction principles (le_ind) reflecting those defining clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use constructors as hints (Hint Resolve le_n le_S) to help automation. For proofs that require analyzing which constructor applies to a hypothesis, use inversion_clear or inversion to inspect and extract constructor data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use inversion/inversion_clear to analyze hypotheses built from inductive predicates
rubrics_metrics.description: When a hypothesis is an instance of an inductive predicate, use 'inversion' or 'inversion_clear' to match it against constructors and obtain equalities or sub-hypotheses; helpful to prove uniqueness/trivial cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to show 'le n 0 -> n = 0' use 'inversion_clear H' to see that only the base constructor applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module/library management: Require/Load/Require Export and compiled .vo files
rubrics_metrics.description: Load modules with 'Require Import Module.' or 'Load file.' Compiling .v files to .vo (coqc) makes future loading faster. Use 'Require Export' to re-export dependencies from a module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Libraries map to filesystem directories and are registered with Add LoadPath. Use absolute names (Coq.Arith.Arith) to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Search, SearchAbout and SearchPattern to find lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Use SearchAbout to lookup facts concerning a predicate, Search to find lemmas where the predicate appears at the head of the conclusion, and SearchPattern with '_' wildcards to match conclusion patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'SearchAbout le.', 'Search le.', 'SearchPattern (_ + _ = _).' These tools help discover existing lemmas to avoid reproving common facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage proof scripts: Save/Abort/Restart/Undo/Inspect
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Save name' records the current proof as a named lemma (or Save uses prior Goal name), Abort discards the current proof and returns to main loop, Restart restarts proof of the same lemma, Undo n backtracks n steps, Inspect n lists last n declared notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Save to store successful proofs; Inspect helps review recently declared items. Abort and Restart help interactively exploring different proof strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the context clean: clear unused hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove unnecessary hypotheses with 'clear' to declutter the context and ease reading and automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., after moving HA into context you may clear an unused H to simplify later steps. This is especially helpful in large developments to avoid confusing or ambiguous names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of constructivity: not all classically valid transformations hold without axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classically valid equalities or implications (e.g., Peirce's law) are not provable constructively; their double negations may be provable but the direct classical statement requires importing classical axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need classical reasoning, either Require Import Classical or assume excluded middle instances; document such dependencies since they affect extracted programs and computational content.

rubrics_metrics.name: When defining/proving, prefer using library-provided Prelude definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you redefine standard types (bool, nat, plus) during experimentation, reset to Prelude definitions (Reset bool) before continuing to avoid confusing error messages from redeclarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard library definitions for compatibility with other lemmas and automation. Redefinitions are useful for learning but undesirable in long-term developments.
